description: Real-world base rates behind the synthetic layer event frequencies (spec section c). Each rate is sourced, or says plainly that it is assumed. Referenced by rules.v1.json#base_rates_file.

base_rates.quantity: probability a buyer-side champion leaves the employer during one deal window
base_rates.real_value: median tenure with current employer 4.9 years for management, professional and related occupations (January 2026; 4.8 in January 2024)

source.title: BLS, Employee Tenure in January 2026 (released 2026-09-24)
source.quote: workers in management, professional, and related occupations had the highest median tenure in January 2026 (4.9 years)

base_rates.derivation: Constant hazard ln2/4.9 = 0.141 per year gives 1 - exp(-0.141 * 0.25) = 3.5% per 90-day window. Amplified to 12% so that roughly 140 deals carry the event (statistical power). Champions are not a random sample of managers, so this is an order of magnitude, not a calibration.

base_rates.quantity: annual CEO departures in large listed companies
base_rates.real_value: 58 S&P 500 CEO departures in 2024 (11.6% of 500 companies)

source.title: Russell Reynolds Associates, Record number of CEOs left their roles in 2024
source.quote: The S&P 500 losing 58 CEOs last year - a 21% increase on 2023 and the second highest on record.

base_rates.synthetic_target: a new executive joins the account on 10% of deals (any executive, not only the CEO)
base_rates.derivation: 11.6% per year is 2.9% per 90-day window for the CEO alone; other officers add to it. 10% per deal window is assumed and amplified.

base_rates.quantity: frequency of officer departures and appointments disclosed on Form 8-K Item 5.02

source.title: SEC Form 8-K, Item 5.02 (Departure of Directors or Certain Officers; Election of Directors; Appointment of Certain Officers; Compensatory Arrangements of Certain Officers)
source.quote: Unless otherwise specified, a report is to be filed or furnished within four business days after occurrence of the event.

base_rates.derivation: Not computed. Item 5.02 is the right public base rate for officer changes, but we did not count filings per filer-year. Counting EDGAR Item 5.02 filings is an open question for the lead; the Russell Reynolds CEO rate stands in until then.

base_rates.quantity: probability a company runs an organisational redesign in a given period
base_rates.real_value: 82% of respondents had experienced a redesign at their current company; 70% of those said the most recent one was within the past two years

source.title: McKinsey Global Survey, The secrets of successful organizational redesigns

base_rates.synthetic_target: a reorganisation touching the buying group during 22% of deals
base_rates.derivation: 0.82 * 0.70 = 57% within two years, about 0.42 per year, about 10% per 90-day window. A company-wide redesign is broader than a change touching one buying group, and the figures come from a search-result summary (our fetch of the page timed out), so confidence is low.

base_rates.quantity: people involved in a complex B2B purchase
base_rates.synthetic_target: every account gets one champion, one economic buyer, at most one separate decision maker, at least one technical evaluator; the rest are end users (about 9 contacts per account)
base_rates.derivation: Widely quoted Gartner figure; the Gartner page returned HTTP 403 to our fetch, so the number is taken as quoted, not re-read.

base_rates.quantity: buyer-side people engaged in won versus lost deals
base_rates.real_value: closed-won deals often involve at least three buyer-side players; lost ones often only one

source.title: Gong, How to win mega-deals: a guide to multi-threading done right
source.quote: closed-won deals often involve the active participation of at least three key players from the buyer's side

base_rates.derivation: Vendor data and correlational. The planted odds ratio is assumed; only the threshold of three is taken from the source.

base_rates.quantity: share of deals where a new buyer-side person joins mid-deal
base_rates.derivation: Assumed. Chosen so the champion-kept and champion-bypassed arms both have enough deals.

base_rates.quantity: share of deals where the champion changes role inside the account
base_rates.derivation: Assumed; counted with departures for syn1_champion_gone_unreplaced when the new role is away from the deal.

base_rates.quantity: share of replacement owners who are acting or interim
base_rates.synthetic_target: 40% of replacements, acting for 30 to 90 days

base_rates.quantity: probability a buyer replies to an outbound email inside an active deal, where no real customer email covers that period
base_rates.real_value: 2,245 of 5,177 CRMArena-Pro emails (43.4%) were sent by customers (WP31 loader, direction from the sender; the Incoming flag is false on all of them); all 507 'Re:' emails link to an earlier email
base_rates.synthetic_target: real customer emails are base data and are never duplicated or contradicted; synthetic replies fill only outbound emails with no real customer email before the next outbound, at 35% at neutral health (kinds 55% positive, 20% objection, 25% timing request)
base_rates.derivation: The 43.4% customer share is measured. The 35% fill rate and the kind mix for uncovered periods are assumed.

base_rates.quantity: share of closed opportunities that are won
base_rates.derivation: Assumed for statistical power. We found no absolute B2B win-rate figure we could verify from a primary source (the Ebsta/Pavilion H1 2024 deck reports relative changes only).
